segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came down from the mountain, large crowds followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, a man with a skin disease came up and bowed down before him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if you are willing, you can cleanse me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am willing. Be cleansed.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately his skin disease was cleansed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he entered Capernaum, a centurion came up to him, begging him

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, my servant is lying at home paralyzed, terribly tormented.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I will come and cure him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the centurion answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, I am not fit to have you come under my roof. But only say the word, and my servant will be healed.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes, and to my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus heard this, he was amazed and said to those following him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I tell you that many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of the heavens,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but the sons of the kingdom will be thrown out into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to the centurion,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go. Let it be done for you as you have believed.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the servant was healed in that very hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus came into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying in bed with a fever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, they brought to him many who were demon-possessed, and he drove out the spirits with a word and cured all who were sick,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “He himself took our sicknesses and carried our diseases.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus saw large crowds around him, he gave orders to go across to the other side.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a scribe came up and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Another of the disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he got into a boat, his disciples followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, a great storm arose on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was sleeping.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came and woke him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, save us! We are perishing!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you such cowards, you of little faith?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he got up and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The people were amazed, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What kind of person is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came to the other side, to the region of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs. They were so fierce that no one was able to pass along that road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, they cried out, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you want with us, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now at a distance from them a large herd of pigs was feeding.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The demons begged him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you drive us out, send us into the herd of pigs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they came out and went off into the pigs, and look, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and died in the waters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those tending them fled, went off into the town, and reported everything, including what had happened to the demon-possessed men.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, the whole town came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him they begged him to leave their region.

notes.phrase: a man with a skin disease
notes.note: The Greek word names someone with the ritually defiling skin condition regulated in Leviticus 13–14, a range of scaly conditions that made a person unclean, which is why the man asks to be “cleansed” and not simply healed. “Leper” today means a person with Hansen’s disease, which is narrower than the Greek term and may not be included in it. Most translations keep “leper” and explain it in a footnote; scholars widely agree the biblical term is broader.

The verb names the act of prostrating oneself in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it: a god, a king, or a superior from whom one seeks a favor. Here a petitioner approaches Jesus with no confession of divine status, so the gesture itself is rendered. The KJV has “worshipped”; most modern versions have “knelt before him.” Scholars disagree about how much divine recognition Matthew intends in such scenes.

Leviticus 14 requires a person recovered from such a skin disease to be examined by a priest and to bring offerings before rejoining the community. “Them” may be the priests or the people at large, and the “testimony” may be proof that the man is clean, evidence that Jesus upholds the Law of Moses, or both. The Greek does not settle the question.

The Greek word can mean “child,” “boy,” “son” or “servant.” Most translations choose “servant” because the parallel account in Luke 7:2 calls him a slave, but some scholars think Matthew means the centurion’s son. Matthew uses a different word, rendered “slave,” in verse 9.

notes.phrase: I will come and cure him.
notes.traditional: I will come and heal him.
notes.note: The Greek has an emphatic “I” and can equally be read as a question: “Am I to come and cure him?” On that reading Jesus voices a Jew’s hesitation about entering a Gentile’s house, and the centurion’s reply in verse 8 answers the objection. Most translations take it as a statement; a number of commentators prefer the question.

The Greek word means “sufficient,” “adequate” or “fit”; it is not the ordinary word for “worthy.” It is the word John the Baptist uses in Matthew 3:11 of his unfitness to carry the coming one’s sandals. Most translations have “worthy” or “I do not deserve.”

Manuscripts differ here. The reading translated is “with no one in Israel have I found such faith”; many manuscripts read “not even in Israel have I found such faith,” which matches Luke 7:9 and may have been copied from there. The difference is of emphasis more than substance.

Matthew’s Greek has the plural, “heavens,” reflecting Hebrew and Aramaic, in which the word is always plural. The phrase is Matthew’s usual equivalent of “the kingdom of God” in the other Gospels. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”; the plural is kept here as a Semitic turn of phrase a first-century hearer would have noticed.

“Sons of” something is a Semitic idiom for those who belong to it or stand to inherit it. Here it means those who expected a place by right at the banquet of the age to come, pictured in verse 11 as reclining at a feast with the patriarchs. Some translations paraphrase as “heirs” or “subjects” of the kingdom.
The quotation is Isaiah 53:4. Matthew’s wording is closer to the Hebrew than to the Greek Septuagint, which speaks of bearing “sins,” and he applies the line to Jesus’s physical healings.

notes.phrase: leave the dead to bury their own dead
notes.note: Burying a parent was among the most binding family duties in Jewish society and in the ancient world generally, so the saying is deliberately shocking. The “dead” who are to do the burying are usually understood as those who are not alive to the kingdom. Some interpreters think the father had not yet died and the man was asking to stay home until he did, but this is disputed.

The Greek word means “a shaking” and ordinarily refers to an earthquake; Matthew uses it that way at Jesus’s death and resurrection (27:54; 28:2). Used of the sea it denotes a violent storm, and the parallel accounts in Mark and Luke use a word for a windstorm. The “great storm” is answered by the “great calm” of verse 26.
The Greek adjective means “cowardly” or “timid” and is a term of reproach, stronger than the ordinary vocabulary for fear. Most translations soften it to “afraid” or “fearful.”

Manuscripts vary among “Gadarenes,” “Gerasenes” and “Gergesenes,” both here and in the parallel accounts in Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26. “Gadarenes” is the best-supported reading in Matthew; Gadara was a city of the Decapolis some miles southeast of the lake whose territory seems to have reached the shore. The KJV, following later manuscripts, has “Gergesenes.”
